ABSTRACT
This study presents a novel optimization strategy, called the transient simulation-response surface method-life
cycle assessment (TRS-RSM-LCA), for the optimal design of a trigeneration or combined cooling, heat, and
power (CCHP) system incorporating solar collectors and hydrogen generation subsystems. The TRS-RSM-LCA
aims to achieve the optimal energy, economic, and environmental (3E) design of the proposed hybrid energy
system throughout its lifespan. The optimization study considers the solar collector area and fuel cell capacity as
numeric factors, and the solar collector type and cooling system type as categoric factors. The study investigates
the interactions among these design parameters and their impact on the 3E indicators. Results demonstrate that
the optimized CCHP system significantly outperforms the base system. The optimized system achieves a 58 %
reduction in net electricity consumption (7581.6 kWh) compared to the base system (18,051.6 kWh). Moreover,
it exhibits a 38.2 % decrease in net natural gas consumption, a 39.5 % reduction in life cycle cost, and a 46.3 %
reduction in 100-year global warming potential. The comparative analysis findings provide valuable insights for
decision-makers, enabling them to evaluate the overall system performance and understand the trade-offs
involved in optimizing multiple factors.

1. Introduction
Global energy consumption continues to rise significantly, driven by
population growth and industrialization, resulting in increased green-
house gas emissions and intensifying the urgency for sustainable energy
solutions [ 1 ]. Combined cooling, heat, and power (CCHP) systems, also
known as trigeneration systems, are essential for the optimal integration
of renewable energy sources in residential apartment communities [ 2 ].
These innovative systems combine electricity generation, heating, and
cooling into a single process, utilizing a variety of energy sources such as
solar power, wind energy, or biomass [ 3 ]. The incorporation of renew-
able energy sources into CCHP systems reduces reliance on fossil fuels
[ 4 ]. The considerable energy consumption of such areas emphasizes the
need to research and deploy CCHP systems in residential communities.
Residential buildings, for example, account for over 40 % of total global
energy usage [ 5 ]. By optimizing energy production, storage, and dis-
tribution, CCHP systems can significantly contribute to reducing energy
costs, enhancing energy efficiency, and mitigating environmental im-
pacts for residential apartment communities [ 6 ].
Complex hybrid systems require careful analysis and fine-tuning
because of their numerous interdependent components and varied en-
ergy sources [ 7 ]. Researchers can determine the best types of equip-
ment, their capacities, and control schemes through optimization, which
maximizes energy use and minimizes energy waste [ 8 ]. For instance,
Ren et al. [ 9 ] proposes hybrid CCHP system, which is equipped with a
gas turbine, water storage tank, absorption unit, ground source heat
pump, photovoltaic panels (PV), solar thermal collectors, batteries, and
photovoltaic/thermal collectors (PVT). The evaluation is done on two

heat collector enhances the energy efficiency. Using the primary energy
saving ratio (PESR) and yearly cost saving ratio (CSR) as the goal of
optimization study, Song et al. [ 12 ] performs an optimization study of a
CCHP system integrated with solar energy. Their optimization outcomes
indicate a contradiction among fuel economy and cost reduction. The
average PESR rises to around 37.9 %, and the average CSR rises to 25 %,
approximately, when the constrained optimum point is chosen.
A statistical method for optimizing hybrid energy systems is called
response surface method (RSM). To predict the relationship between
input variables and intended responses, RSM builds a mathematical
model [ 13 ]. In order to find the best solutions for hybrid energy systems,
RSM makes it possible to explore the design space systematically [ 14 ].
Saedpanah et al. [ 15 ] developed an optimization method to achieve the
best possible layout of a hybrid air conditioning system, which consists
of a thermal energy storage, a desiccant wheel, PVT panels, ground
source heat exchanger, and absorption chiller. Their findings demon-
strated that the system ’ s yearly natural gas and electrical power usage,
applying the optimal design discovered by RSM, decreased by 51.8 %
and 14.6 %, respectively. Mao et al. [ 16 ] used RSM to accelerate the
computer modeling process to estimate the interior temperature envi-
ronment. They compared the findings from the numerical technique
(RSM method) alongside the computational fluid dynamics (CFD)
approach in order to examine the energy efficiency and thermal comfort
conditions of a bedroom tac unit. Tooryan et al. [ 17 ] investigated the
optimal design and energy management of a hybrid microgrid system
with distributed energy resources. The study proposes an approach to
minimize operational costs by incorporating photovoltaic arrays, bat-
tery energy storage, fuel cells, thermal energy storage, and boilers. They
explored the utilization of residential and municipal waste for electricity
generation, along with load growth considerations. They employed
Particle Swarm Optimization Algorithm to determine the best energy
management strategy and resource capacity. Their results showed re-
ductions in natural gas consumption by fuel cells (6.2 % with residential
waste and 26.7 % with residential and municipal waste) and a signifi-
cant decrease in CO

cell heat. Nedaei et al. [ 18 ] studied the design and optimization of a
hybrid power system. The system ’ s objective is to produce electricity
from wind power. If there is excess electricity, it may be utilized to
produce hydrogen on a small scale or transferred to the grid for medium-
or large-scale electrification. Their results showed that the estimated
daily wind energy production transmitted to the grid is around 2000
kWh. By adjusting the hybrid energy system and considering various
design coefficients such as electricity price, hydrogen production,
hydrogen price, and electricity transmitted to the grid, the study finds
that the net monthly revenues can reach a maximum level of € 1974.87.
The need for sustainable and efficient energy systems has intensified
due to rising environmental concerns, the increasing demand for energy,
and the need for economically viable solutions in urban areas. Combined
cooling, heating, and power (CCHP) systems, which can integrate
renewable energy sources, present a promising avenue for meeting these
demands, especially in dense residential communities. However, opti-
mizing these systems remains a complex challenge that requires
balancing multiple objectives — energy efficiency, economic feasibility,
and environmental sustainability — each influenced by various system
components and configurations.
Current literature reveals significant gaps in understanding the
optimization of hybrid CCHP systems for maximal performance across
these three pillars. Specifically.
• Research Gap #1: Existing studies primarily focus on multi-objective
optimization for CCHP systems, but often neglect to explore different
weighting schemes or decision-making techniques that could prior-
itize energy, economic, or environmental objectives more effec-
tively. Analyzing these trade-offs with alternative approaches could
yield valuable insights into the performance boundaries and poten-
tial compromises in CCHP system design.
• Research Gap #2: Previous studies have not yet examined the
simultaneous optimization of solar collector type and cooling system
type within hybrid CCHP systems. While some research addresses
these elements in isolation, a holistic approach that considers their
combined impact is essential to advancing the energy efficiency and
sustainability of hybrid CCHP systems.
• Research Gap #3: The life cycle assessment (LCA) of hybrid CCHP
systems — accounting for environmental impacts such as embodied
energy, emissions, and waste generation throughout the system ’ s
lifecycle — remains underexplored. A comprehensive LCA could
provide critical insights into the long-term sustainability of these
systems and inform environmentally responsible design choices.
To address these gaps, this study introduces a novel transient
simulation-response surface method-life cycle assessment (TRS-RSM-
LCA) framework for the hybrid CCHP system, designed to optimize
component configuration while balancing energy, economic, and envi-
ronmental (3E) objectives. This approach not only simulates time-
dependent heat transfer and thermodynamics but also provides a
nuanced understanding of the system ’ s environmental impacts across its
lifecycle. Using TRNSYS for transient simulations, RSM for design of
experiments, and LCA for evaluating lifecycle impacts, this strategy aims
to identify an optimal system configuration for a residential apartment
community. A subsequent trade-off analysis further contextualizes these
findings, offering practical insights for stakeholders on how best to
balance the 3E objectives in real-world applications.
2. Materials and methods
This section presents the description of the system, modeling, and
optimization methodology used in this study.
2.1. Description of system
The hybrid system described consists of five major subsystems: the
hydrogen generation subsystem, hot water storage subsystem, solar
subsystem, cooling subsystem, and controller subsystem. Each subsys-
tem plays a crucial role in the overall operation and efficiency of the
system.
The hydrogen generation subsystem comprises an electrolyzer, a
compressor, a hydrogen storage tank, and a fuel cell system. This sub-
system is responsible for generating electricity through the process of
electrolysis, where water is split into hydrogen and oxygen. The
generated hydrogen is stored in a tank, and a fuel cell converts it back
into electricity when needed. Additionally, the fuel cell can utilize the
heat produced during its operation to heat a stream of water, which is

then returned to the hot water storage tank.
The hot water storage subsystem includes a hot water storage tank
and a backup boiler. The storage tank has multiple inlets and outlets,
with each serving a specific purpose. The first inlet and outlet are con-
nected to the fuel cell subsystem, allowing the transfer of heated water
between the fuel cell and the storage tank. The second inlet and outlet
are linked to the solar subsystem, enabling the transfer of solar-heated
water to the storage tank. The third inlet and outlet are associated
with the cooling subsystem (specifically, if level 2 of the cooling sub-
system is chosen), allowing the transfer of hot water from the storage
tank to fulfill the cooling demand. Lastly, the fourth inlet and outlet are
connected to the backup boiler, which is responsible for increasing the
temperature of the tank water to meet the hot water consumption needs
of the apartment complex.
The solar subsystem offers three levels in the decision-making pro-
cess: level 1 utilizes an evacuated tube collector (ETC), level 2 employs a
parabolic trough collector (PTC), and level 3 incorporates a photovol-
taic/thermal collector (PVT). The solar subsystem ’ s primary function is
to raise the water temperature in the hot water storage tank using the
available solar radiation. The selection of the appropriate solar system
type is determined through an optimization methodology, which is
discussed in detail in the paper.
The cooling subsystem is designed to meet the cooling demand of the
apartment complex. It offers two levels: level 1 utilizes an air-source
heat pump (HP), and level 2 incorporates an absorption chiller (AC).
The level 1 HP system operates by extracting heat from the ambient
outdoor air and transferring it to the indoor space, effectively providing
cooling. The HP utilizes a refrigeration cycle, driven by electricity, to
facilitate this heat transfer process. By leveraging the temperature dif-
ference between the indoor and outdoor air, the HP can provide efficient
cooling without the need for a direct thermal energy input. If the level 2
AC system is chosen during the decision-making process, the required
thermal energy for the AC generator is provided by extracting a hot
water stream from the hot water storage tank. This integration enables
the utilization of waste heat from the system to fulfill the cooling re-
quirements, further enhancing the overall energy efficiency. The key
difference between the level 1 HP system and the level 2 AC system is the
source of thermal energy used to drive the cooling process. While the
level 2 AC system relies on the waste heat extracted from the hot water
storage tank, the level 1 HP system uses electricity to power the
compressor and facilitate the heat transfer. The selection between the
level 1 HP and level 2 AC systems is determined through the optimiza-
tion methodology described in the paper. This decision-making process
takes into account factors such as the available solar thermal energy, the
cooling demand, the system efficiency, and the overall energy con-
sumption and cost implications. The optimization aims to select the most
appropriate cooling subsystem configuration to maximize the energy
efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and environmental sustainability of the
overall system.
The controller subsystem plays a crucial role in managing the elec-
tricity consumption and generation of the entire hybrid system. It is
responsible for monitoring and controlling the electricity flow based on
the electricity generated by the fuel cell subsystem and level 3 of the
solar subsystem, as well as the electricity demand of the apartment
complex. The controller subsystem makes decisions regarding the
amount of electricity available for sale to the grid or the amount of
electricity that needs to be purchased from the grid.
2.2. System modeling
To simulate an advanced hybrid CCHP system that integrates solar
energy and hydrogen generation technologies, Transient System Simu-
lation Tool (TRNSYS) and the Fortran programming language are used.
The TRNSYS and Thermal Energy System Specialists (TESS) libraries
offer a wide range of Fortran-coded components (i.e., Types) that are
effectively integrated with TRNSYS to model the proposed system.
TRNSYS had been chosen as the main modeling program due to its
established credibility in the research community [ 19 ]. Moreover,
certain experimental studies have verified the dependability of the
Fortran codes used in TRNSYS Types [ 20 – 26 ].
The performance characteristics of the evacuated tube solar collector
(ETC) are determined by utilizing Eq. (1) to calculate the thermal effi-
ciency [ 27 ]. This equation is implemented within Type 71 of the
TRNSYS software, where this component effectively models the
behavior of ETC by employing a standard quadratic efficiency equation.
Type 1245 of the TESS library is employed to determine the behavior of
the parabolic trough solar collector (PTC). This particular component
effectively models a medium-temperature non-tracking concentrating
parabolic solar collector, taking into account the influence of collector
mass on performance. PTC collectors consist of an evacuated tube con-
taining an absorber and heat transfer fluid, with an external reflective
concentrator located at the back. The model calculates the collector fin
efficiency (F ′ ) to determine the collector loss coefficient and the
transmittance-absorptance product at normal incidence, as depicted in
Eq. (2) [ 28 ]. Type 560 of the TRNSYS software, utilized in various
studies such as [ 15 , 29 , 30 ], is specifically designed to model PVT panels.
This model enables the calculation of both the fluid temperature at the
collector outlet and the generated power by utilizing Eqs. (3) and (4)
[ 31 ]. The Type 560 model employs linear variables to establish the
correlation between photovoltaic effectiveness, cell temperature, and
incident solar radiation. However, it does not incorporate degradation
factors into its calculations.
Type 966 from the TESS library is employed to analyze the charac-
teristics of a heat pump (HP). This particular model utilizes a set of
empirical coefficients to accurately represent the behavior of an air-to-
air heat pump [ 32 ]. By considering the entering evaporator air wet
bulb temperature and the condenser air dry bulb temperature, Type 966
calculates various parameters such as total and sensible capacity, energy
efficiency ratio (EIR), and bypass fraction at the current inlet conditions.
Eq. (5) (8) [ 28 ] are incorporated within Type 966 to facilitate the
modeling of the heat pump (HP). To model the behavior of the ab-
sorption chiller (AC), the study utilizes Type 107 of the TRNSYS soft-
ware. Within this component, Eqs. (9) and (10) [ 32 ] are used to
determine the outlet temperature of the hot water stream from the
generator and the cooling water stream, respectively.
In order to simulate fuel cells, Type 173 is utilized, incorporating Eq.
(11) (17) from Refs. [ 27 , 33 ]. For the accurate simulation of the elec-
trolyzer and its hydrogen production, Type 160 of the TRNSYS software
is employed, with Eq. (18) defining the ultimate rate of hydrogen pro-
duction [ 27 ]. It is important to acknowledge that the density of con-
nected cells directly impacts the hydrogen production rate of the
electrolyzer.
The governing equations for other components such as backup
boiler, pumps, fans, compressor, and storage tanks are not presented
here due to the extensive number of equations involved. However, these
equations are fully considered to ensure accurate simulations, and they
can be found in Ref. [ 27 ].
The following main assumptions are incorporated into the applied
mathematical model, based on the referenced resources.
• The radial conductive thermal resistance of the pipes is considered
imperceptible in the model [ 19 ].
• Radial heat conduction is not taken into account in the model [ 34 ].
• In the electrolyzer subsystem Hydrogen and air are assumed to be
ideal gases [ 29 ].
• The water used as heat transfer fluid is considered to be an incom-
pressible fluid [ 27 , 35 ].
• The model for the evacuated tube solar collector assumes that the
relationship between efficiency and the ratio of the temperature
difference between the fluid and ambient temperature to the radia-
tion curve can be represented by a quadratic equation [ 28 ].

2.3. Optimization methodology
The primary objective of this study is to develop an optimization
strategy for a hybrid CCHP system that integrates solar energy and
hydrogen generation (see Fig. 1 ). The aim is to achieve optimal energy,
economic, and environmental (3E) performance throughout the sys-
tem ’ s lifespan. Nevertheless, traditional optimization methods are

2.7. Overview of the TRS-RSM-LCA methodology
The primary objective of this study is to develop an optimization
strategy for a hybrid CCHP system, integrating solar energy and
hydrogen generation to maximize energy, economic, and environmental
(3E) performance over the system ’ s lifecycle. The TRS-RSM-LCA
approach combines three complementary methods.
1. Transient Simulation (TRS): TRS is applied to capture the system ’ s
dynamic behavior over time, which is essential for accurately
modeling and evaluating performance under real-world operating
conditions. The simulations are conducted over time intervals
ranging from seconds to hours to account for varying load demands
and energy fluctuations, enabling detailed 3E assessment.
2. Response Surface Method (RSM): RSM reduces the computational
demands of extensive simulations by creating a response surface
model that predicts system behavior. Using central composite design
(CCD), RSM facilitates the exploration of multiple scenarios with
minimal simulation runs, effectively balancing accuracy with
computational efficiency.
3. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA): LCA evaluates the environmental
impact of the system throughout its lifespan — from raw material
extraction to disposal. This holistic approach provides insight into
the environmental costs, such as emissions and resource depletion, of
different system configurations and operational strategies.
The integration of these three methods provides a streamlined
optimization framework that is both time-efficient and comprehensive,
significantly reducing computational demands compared to traditional
methods.

meet demand fluctuations.

The results of this study have significant implications for both policy
and practice in optimizing combined cooling, heating, and power
(CCHP) systems integrated with renewable energy. The findings
demonstrate that prioritizing different objectives (e.g., electricity sav-
ings, natural gas reduction, cost-efficiency, or environmental sustain-
ability) can lead to substantial trade-offs in performance metrics such as
costs, environmental impact, and fuel consumption. For policymakers,
these insights emphasize the importance of developing flexible, multi-
criteria frameworks that allow stakeholders to balance energy effi-
ciency, cost savings, and environmental goals. This multi-objective
approach can aid in formulating policies that incentivize energy opti-
mization while minimizing the negative impacts associated with prior-
itizing a single metric over others.

decision-makers in energy systems to tailor CCHP configurations based
on specific operational goals. For example, in regions where electricity
scarcity is a primary concern, prioritizing electricity reduction may be
advisable despite potential increases in natural gas use and costs.
Alternatively, in areas where environmental sustainability is prioritized,
decision-makers may choose configurations that minimize greenhouse
gas emissions, even at the expense of slightly higher costs or energy use.
Overall, the study offers a framework that can be adapted to different
regional or organizational priorities, allowing energy system designers
and operators to make informed decisions that align with both policy
goals and real-world constraints.

3.7. Future research direction
Future research could focus on exploring additional design param-
eters, such as varying types of renewable energy sources and storage
options, to further enhance the flexibility and resilience of CCHP sys-
tems. Additionally, applying the TRS-RSM-LCA methodology to other
hybrid systems or in different climatic regions could offer valuable in-
sights into regional optimization strategies. Finally, incorporating
advanced optimization techniques, such as machine learning algo-
rithms, could enhance the accuracy and computational efficiency of the
optimization process, providing a more comprehensive approach to
sustainable energy system design.
4. Conclusions
In conclusion, this paper introduced the transient simulation-
response surface method-life cycle assessment (TRS-RSM-LCA) as a
groundbreaking optimization strategy for designing combined cooling,
heat, and power (CCHP) systems that integrate solar collectors and
hydrogen generation subsystems. This innovative approach not only
targets the optimal energy, economic, and environmental (3E) perfor-
mance of hybrid energy systems over their lifespan but also contributes
meaningfully to the broader discourse on sustainable energy solutions.
By addressing critical global energy challenges—such as the need for
increased energy efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas emissions—the
findings from this study underscore the potential of CCHP systems to
enhance energy security and sustainability. The optimization process
considered both numerical factors, like solar collector area and fuel cell
capacity, and categorical factors, including types of solar collectors and
cooling systems. The TRS-RSM-LCA methodology successfully combined
transient simulation, response surface method, and life cycle
assessment, creating a robust framework for optimizing hybrid energy
systems.
The results revealed that the optimized CCHP system achieved a
remarkable 49.5 % reduction in annual electricity consumption
compared to the baseline configuration, demonstrating significant ad-
vancements in all 3E objectives. This study emphasized the importance
of understanding interactions among design parameters and their effects
on sustainability indicators. Additionally, the analysis of competing
priorities offered valuable insights into potential synergies and conflicts,
guiding stakeholders in comprehensive performance evaluations.
The optimal system configuration, identified through TRS-RSM-LCA,
featured a solar collector area of 213.39 m
2
, a fuel cell capacity of 28.35
kW, a photovoltaic/thermal (PVT) solar collector type, and an absorp-
tion chiller cooling system. This configuration produced favorable out-
comes regarding net energy production, natural gas consumption, life
cycle costs, and greenhouse gas emissions.
Overall, this research not only advances the design of CCHP systems
by providing an effective optimization strategy but also serves as a vital
resource for stakeholders committed to achieving efficient, sustainable
hybrid energy systems that can address pressing global energy
challenges.
